fields.sample_size: semi-structured interviews with 93 Ugandan local government actors (47 political/elected and 46 technical/appointed) at all hierarchical levels across 22 sub-counties in three districts, plus the 2019 Ministry of Water and Environment policy documents
fields.effect_estimate: Uganda's 2019 policy on professionalised maintenance shifted local government responsibilities, but interviewees seldom cited regulative influences (formal rules and policies); actions were driven by normative and cultural-cognitive influences (relationship expectations, routines, political dynamics, identity), so the policy alone is unlikely to secure local government support unless allocated responsibilities align with those influences. Qualitative coding; no effect estimates.
fields.study_design: qualitative multiple-case study (93 interviews across 22 sub-counties and three districts; policy document analysis)
fields.section: Full text: Methods (interview data collection, 93 respondents); Results (regulative, normative, cultural-cognitive influences); Conclusions
fields.exact_location: Methods (interview data collection, 93 respondents); Results (regulative, normative, cultural-cognitive influences); Conclusions

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: 93 interviews with local government actors in 22 Ugandan sub-counties (three districts), read in full text 2026-10-04. Formal rules and policies were rarely cited as motivators; normative and cultural-cognitive influences drove support for professionalised maintenance, so the 2019 policy alone is unlikely to ensure support.
notes: Abstract-level extraction accurate; adds n = 93 (47 political, 46 technical), 22 sub-counties. Direct evidence that regulative (legal) levers alone do not shape local government behaviour.
